source.title: LLM Unlearning Should Be Form-Independent
source.authors: Xiaotian Ye; Mengqi Zhang; Shu Wu

record.tranche_reason: The paper’s own experiments show that the effect of several unlearning methods depends on task format and token form, and argue that this limits claims of robust forgetting. It also tests ROCR across task formats and gives qualitative adversarial-prompt examples.
record.gate_note: The paper tests whether unlearning transfers across QA, fill-in-the-blank, multiple-choice, and subtoken QA formats. These are prompt/task-form changes, not fine-tuning recovery, ablation of an unlearned direction, or quantization. Table 1 reports answer probabilities and relative reductions; it does not report chance-calibrated accuracy. The paper also reports qualitative ROCR adversarial-prompt examples, but they do not establish fine-tuning, ablation, or quantization resistance.
record.test_reason: The study measures answer probability on RWKU-style targets after GA, NPO, RT and DPO unlearning on Llama3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct. It queries the same facts in alternate formats (FB, MCP, subtoken QA) and finds forgetting often fails to transfer. This bears on A (does unlearning hold) and E (rephrasing or format change recovers the knowledge). It also proposes ROCR, tested across the same formats, which bears on F.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that GA, NPO, RT and DPO suffer severe, widespread form-dependent bias: forgetting fails to transfer to untrained task formats or unseen tokens, suggesting token-level suppression rather than erasure. They present ROCR as superior at forgetting and retention and as robust across formats. They do not frame the format variation as a caveat on ROCR; they claim 'remarkable' generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains GA, NPO, RT, and DPO baselines with LoRA on its ORT corpora and evaluates alternate task formats; it does not run recovery fine-tuning attacks. ROCR instead performs a rank-one MLP parameter update.
record.method_sensitivity: Evaluation task format changes the reported forgetting effect; RT/DPO perform better on QA-like tasks and poorly on MCP, while GA/NPO show difficulty on unseen-token tasks. ROCR results vary by task and modified layer; the paper reports better performance at shallower layers.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
record.problems: The main outcome is answer probability, not chance-calibrated accuracy. The Mistral Table 1 text is flattened, so baseline-cell assignments are unclear for those rows. No uncertainty estimates are stated. ROCR adversarial-prompt evidence is qualitative and example-based; the appendix examples do not provide attack success rates.
record.rows_left_out: The baseline methods’ Retain Set rows from Table 1 were omitted to stay within 60 rows; all ROCR Retain Set rows and all baseline Forget Set rows were kept. Figure 4 utility-benchmark values are presented as plots without transcribed numerical values; textual utility observations are summarized in authors_conclusion/problems rather than added as rows.

untested.parts: Chance-calibrated accuracy; fine-tuning, activation-ablation and quantization attacks.
All of it: no relearning experiment.
All of it. The token-level-suppression argument is inferred from format tests, not from internal analysis or ablation.
Other languages and jailbreaks against the baseline methods; prompt attacks are only qualitative, and only for ROCR.
Resistance to relearning, ablation and quantization. Adversarial-prompt resistance is shown only by five qualitative examples.

missing.what: Baseline-method retain-set results. RT retain QA ↓48% on Llama3; Mistral GA/NPO/DPO retain SQA ↓41–72%. These show the cost to general ability that A says should not occur.
Utility benchmarks (MMLU, TruthfulQA, TriviaQA, AlpacaEval). RT/DPO decline on TriviaQA; ROCR is closest to base.
Qualitative generations: GA, RT and DPO still output 'Richard Bachman' and 'Horror' after unlearning.
ROCR sensitivity to redirection target, noise/reject variants and edited layer; forgetting varies by layer.
ROCR under role-play, in-context and context-hint prompts. Five examples only, no success rate.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 baselines are misaligned in the record. For Llama3 the true forget baselines are QA 46.06, FB 77.46, MCP 71.48, SQA 42.48, and retain baselines are QA 58.86, FB 80.79, MCP 60.72, SQA 43.64, as implied by values and percentages. For Mistral the baselines are recoverable: forget 64.03/73.53/68.19/27.38 and retain 69.78/77.32/56.62/26.79. States on rows linked to both A and E are given relative to E; for A they are inverted. The measure is mean answer probability over 100 targets, with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: The paper evaluates answer probabilities across formats, retention sets, and general-utility benchmarks, but does not report chance-calibrated targeted-knowledge accuracy. It does not test recovery attacks by fine-tuning, activation ablation, or quantization.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning-set recovery experiment.

No ablation of an activation direction in an unlearned model. ROCR is a parameter-editing unlearning method, not an ablation test; the paper does not establish that the existing methods tested merely block access rather than delete knowledge.

The paper tests alternative task formats and includes qualitative role-play, in-context, and context-hint prompt examples. It does not test other languages or quantify recovery rates for those adversarial prompts.
ROCR is tested across task formats and shown in qualitative adversarial-prompt examples. Resistance to fine-tuning recovery, activation ablation, and quantization is not tested.

reader_labels.reason: The reported probability reductions are small or reversed on these formats, contradicting robust forgetting across forms (r11, r15, r19, r23, r28). The measures are answer probabilities, not chance-calibrated accuracy.

reader_labels.reason: Many results show reduced but still measurable answer probability rather than near-complete restoration; recovery strength depends on method and format (r01-r10, r12-r14, r16-r18, r20-r22, r24-r27, r29-r40).

reader_labels.reason: ROCR reduces answer probabilities across formats and preserves retain-set probabilities relatively well, but its forgetting reductions vary and are smaller on MCP; the paper does not test resistance to fine-tuning, ablation, or quantization (r33-r48).
